item.text: {"text":"NextItNet’s original design uses stacked causal dilated convolutions and residual blocks to expand receptive fields while preserving sequence order; it does not establish adaptive forgetting or learned interest boundaries ([original paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf)). Relevant recent work addresses selective history use: DyS4Rec (2025) proposes agent-based skipping of irrelevant interactions ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107134)); ScaleRec (2026) uses multiple temporal scales and adaptive masking to reduce redundant interactions, although its backbone is Transformer-based ([paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104318)). These support investigating selective memory, but do not demonstrate a NextItNet-specific change-point mechanism or gains on the pinned benchmark.\n\nAn older, directly relevant temporal mechanism is MTAM (2020): time-aware gates control information filtering and recurrent state transitions, with current intent querying historical memory ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598)). A family-preserving hypothesis is to learn causal gates on individual dilated convolution taps, conditioned on source/destination features and observed time gaps. A soft boundary gate could attenuate messages crossing inferred context changes, changing effective historical access rather than merely scaling an entire residual block. This is a proposed adaptation, not a verified result from these papers. Keep gates jointly trained inside one NextItNet model per category; compare against fixed receptive fields and simple learned decay using macro validation HR@10. Category sensitivity alone does not establish stale-interest errors."}
